passage: Sunaina had written the call on a sticky note: "Hello, I'd like to order a chocolate cake for Saturday, with 'Happy Birthday Mummy' on top." She had said it in her head maybe forty times. Her thoughts were perfectly clear. It was the moment after the first word that scared her: the pause, the shopkeeper's sigh, the "Hello? Hello?" and the click. "Just message them," Zeenat said, flopping on the bed. "They only take calls." Sunaina stared at the phone. Her hands were cold. She dialled. "H-h-hello. I'd like to order a ch... a chocolate cake." The woman at the bakery didn't sigh. She said, "Sure, what name on top?" Afterwards Sunaina lay back, hands shaking, and grinned at the ceiling. Zeenat threw a pillow at her. "Told you."

qa.q: What did Sunaina want written on top of the cake?
qa.a: Happy Birthday Mummy.

qa.q: What was Sunaina afraid of before making the call?
qa.a: She was afraid of the pause after the first word and the shopkeeper sighing or hanging up, not of what she wanted to say.

qa.q: What made the call a turning point for Sunaina?
qa.a: She chose to dial despite her fear, and the woman at the bakery waited patiently instead of sighing.

qa.q: How might the bakery woman's patience affect Sunaina's next call?
qa.a: It might make the next call feel less frightening, since she now knows some listeners simply wait.

grounding: It shows a teenager who rehearses and avoids phone calls although her thoughts are clear, whose stress is mostly about how others will react.

passage: "Ujjwal? It's midnight. Who are you talking to?" "Nobody, Chetan-bhaiya. Go to sleep." "You're talking to the mirror." Ujjwal sighs. "I'm practising the debate intro. Seventeen times now." "You know the topic better than anyone. I heard you at dinner." "At dinner it's you and Mummy. In class it's forty people, and when I get stuck on the first word, they look at each other. That look. So I just don't put my hand up." "You've got answers in your head all day and you don't say them?" "Every day." Chetan sits on the edge of the bed. "That sounds exhausting." "It is. The words aren't the hard part. The faces are." "Then practise on me tomorrow. I'll do the most boring face in the world." Ujjwal laughs despite himself. "Deal."

qa.q: How many times had Ujjwal practised the debate intro?
qa.a: Seventeen times.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal mean when he says 'The faces are' the hard part?
qa.a: He means he fears how classmates react when he gets stuck, more than the speaking itself.

qa.q: What small step does Chetan offer that could help?
qa.a: He offers to let Ujjwal practise on him tomorrow, with a calm, boring face.

qa.q: What is it like for Chetan to learn his brother stays silent every day?
qa.a: It surprises and saddens him, since he knows Ujjwal is clever, and he realises how tiring it must be.

grounding: It shows a teenager who stays silent in class and rehearses constantly although his thoughts are ready, and whose stress is mostly about others' reactions.

passage: Salma, sixteen, had the answer to the chemistry question before anyone else. She could see it, clear as a formula on the board. She kept her hand down. At home in Hyderabad, when Ammi asked her to call the gas agency, she pretended to be busy until her sister Parveen did it. She rehearsed even simple lines in her head: "One refill, please, for flat 3B." Last month a shopkeeper had smirked while she was stuck on "refill," and she still felt it in her chest. That night Parveen sat beside her. "Your words take longer. Your brain doesn't." Salma swallowed. "It's not the words. It's their faces." Parveen squeezed her hand. "Then let's practise the gas call together, with my face."

qa.q: What line did Salma rehearse for the gas call?
qa.a: She rehearsed "One refill, please, for flat 3B."

qa.q: What does Salma mean when she says "It's their faces"?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and anxious mainly about how people react, like the shopkeeper's smirk, more than about the stutter itself.

qa.q: What step does Parveen offer that could help Salma?
qa.a: She offers to practise the gas call together, so Salma can rehearse with a safe, kind listener.

qa.q: How does Parveen see Salma's ability?
qa.a: She sees that Salma's thinking is quick and clear; only the words take longer to come out.

grounding: Shows a teenager who stays silent, avoids phone calls and rehearses constantly despite clear thoughts, whose stress comes mostly from how others react.

passage:
"Uma, the debate trials are tomorrow. Why didn't you sign up?"
"You know why, Nandini."
"You have the best arguments in class. You wrote my whole rebuttal last year."
"In my head, they're perfect. I've rehearsed every one about fifty times."
"So say them."
"And watch everyone's faces when I get stuck on 'however'? The judges looking at their watches?"
"So it's not the talking. It's them."
Uma nodded, picking at the strap of her bag. "Last year a boy laughed. I still hear it."
"Then I'll sit in the front row. Look at me, not the judges."
Uma was quiet a long time. "You'd really do that?"
"I'd really do that. Sign up."

qa.q: What did Uma write for Nandini last year?
qa.a: She wrote Nandini's whole rebuttal last year.

qa.q: What is Uma most worried about?
qa.a: She is anxious and ashamed about people's reactions, the faces, the judges and a laugh she still remembers, not about her arguments.

qa.q: How does Nandini help Uma face the trials?
qa.a: Nandini points out that the problem is others' reactions, and offers to sit in the front row as a friendly face to look at.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Uma's abilities?
qa.a: Nandini sees her as having the best arguments in class, someone who is already a strong debater in thought.

grounding: Shows a teenager who rehearses constantly and stays silent though her thoughts are ready, whose stress is mostly about how others react.

passage: At seventeen I would do almost anything to avoid a phone call. My name is Maria, and I stutter, mostly on M, which is unlucky. I once walked two kilometres in the rain to a pizza place rather than phone in an order. In class my answers were ready, full sentences, but I'd shrug and say "I don't know." At night I rehearsed tomorrow's conversations, word by word. My cousin Tanuja noticed. "You're not scared of talking," she said. "You're scared of people waiting." She was right. The worst part was never the stuck sound. It was the sigh from the other end of the phone. Knowing that didn't fix everything, but it helped me stop blaming myself.

qa.q: How far did Maria walk to avoid phoning in an order?
qa.a: Maria walked two kilometres in the rain to a pizza place.

qa.q: What was Maria most afraid of, according to Tanuja?
qa.a: Maria was afraid and ashamed of people waiting and reacting, like the sigh on the phone, not of talking itself.

qa.q: How did Tanuja's comment help Maria?
qa.a: It showed Maria that the real stress came from others' reactions, which helped Maria stop self-blame.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt watching Maria avoid calls and answers?
qa.a: Tanuja may have felt concerned and protective, noticing how much effort the avoidance was costing.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoids calls, stays silent and rehearses despite clear thoughts, realising the stress is mostly about others' reactions.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Mrs Nirmala Iyer, Class 9B.
Tanvir scored highest in the written history test, but in class he hardly speaks. I've seen him writing answers in the margin before I finish asking, lips moving, rehearsing. When the office asked him to phone his father about a late pickup, he stood by the phone for five minutes and then asked a friend to call.
Today, when he tried to answer, he got stuck on "Mughal" and two boys smirked. He went red and looked down for the rest of the period.
After class, I spoke to him alone. I told him his answers were some of the best in the class and that I would stop any smirking. I offered written or one-to-one answers when he wanted. I've also called his parents to discuss the school counsellor and a speech therapist.

qa.q: Which word did Tanvir get stuck on today?
qa.a: He got stuck on "Mughal".

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when the two boys smirked?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and embarrassed, going red and looking down for the rest of the period.

qa.q: What did Mrs Iyer do next that could reduce Tanvir's stress?
qa.a: She praised his ideas, promised to stop the smirking, offered written or one-to-one answers and spoke to his parents about a counsellor and a speech therapist.

qa.q: How might the smirking boys' reaction affect Tanvir more than the stuck word itself?
qa.a: Their reaction is what made him hide, so it adds more stress than the speech itself, since his thoughts were clear and ready.

grounding: A teacher notices Tanvir's clear thoughts, silence, avoided phone calls and rehearsing, and that his shame comes more from others' reactions than from speech.
